entries.proposition: The review states its scope as mechanisms of ferroptosis and implications in epilepsy; no search method, inclusion rule or appraisal is described.
entries.snippet: This review article aims to comprehensively explore the mechanistic aspects of ferroptosis and its implications in epilepsy

entries.proposition: Animal evidence is dominated by injected iron or haemoglobin (FeCl3, post-traumatic epilepsy models), not genetic epilepsy models.
entries.snippet: cortical injection of hemoglobin or iron salts (FeCl3) into rats can induce chronic seizures
entries.anchor: 3.1 Potential involvement of ferroptosis mechanisms in the pathogenesis of epilepsy

entries.proposition: The one human iron-status case-control cited is a 130 versus 128 transferrin-saturation comparison (ref 55, a 2001 paper on iron overload without the HFE C282Y mutation).
entries.snippet: researchers analyzed transferrin saturation in 130 patients with epilepsy compared to 128 sex- and age-matched control subjects

entries.proposition: Seizures are said to activate a HIF-1a/HO-1 pathway that raises Fe2+ in hippocampal neurons (ref 60); this is the review's only link to the HIF1A axis.
entries.snippet: Several studies have reported that seizures can activate the hif-1a/HO-1 pathway, leading to abnormal iron metabolism and increased Fe2+ accumulation in hippocampal neurons.

entries.proposition: The authors caution against reading the ferroptosis-epilepsy relation as simply causal.
entries.snippet: it is not advisable to overemphasize the direct causal relationship between epilepsy and ferroptosis.

entries.proposition: Clinical limits stated by the review: no trial of ferroptosis inhibitors in epilepsy exists and imaging or fluid markers are not specific.
entries.snippet: No clinical trials have yet tested ferroptosis inhibitors in epilepsy patients, leaving human efficacy unproven despite promising preclinical data.
entries.anchor: 3.3 Clinical evidence of ferroptosis in human epilepsy

entries.proposition: The only genetic-epilepsy ferroptosis result in the review: patient-derived cells from five childhood epilepsy syndromes responding to EPI-743 (ref 17, mitochondrial-disease-related epilepsy).
entries.snippet: ameliorated ferroptosis in cells derived from patients with five distinct childhood epilepsy syndromes in a dose-dependent manner

entries.proposition: The proposed hippocampal iron MRI threshold is given without a source and the authors state it is not validated in epilepsy.
entries.snippet: setting an iron concentration threshold of >1.2 mg/g to identify high-risk epilepsy patients

entries.proposition: The authors state the AMD-derived diagnostic and delivery ideas are not validated in epilepsy.
entries.snippet: Although these measures have not yet been validated in epilepsy

entries.proposition: Text says valproate decreased lipid peroxides in a kainic acid mouse model (ref 85).
entries.snippet: VPA not only markedly decreased lipid peroxide levels but also suppressed Ptgs2 mRNA expression

entries.proposition: Table 1 describes valproate as leading to non-transferrin-bound iron and elevated oxidative stress, the opposite sign to the text, and cites (87), which in the reference list is a topiramate migraine paper.
entries.snippet: VPA contributes to iron metabolism in epilepsy, leading to the generation of non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI) and an elevation in oxidative stress levels.

entries.proposition: Table 1 attaches reference (55) to a DHEA oxidative-stress statement; ref 55 in the reference list is the iron-overload-without-C282Y epilepsy paper, so citation numbers in the table are not aligned with the list.
entries.snippet: The administration of DHEA has been demonstrated to exert inhibitory effects on lipid peroxidation
Iron overload without the C282Y mutation in patients with epilepsy.

entries.proposition: The review links iron to myelination and catecholamine metabolism in one sentence, without data.
entries.snippet: Additionally, iron closely associates with myelin formation and catecholamine neurotransmitter metabolism in the nervous system (43, 44).

entries.proposition: Figure 1 writes the Fenton reaction as Fe2+ + H2O2 giving Fe3+ + OH- + OH-, with the radical not distinguished from the hydroxide; a diagram, not data.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation - pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 1 (Iron metabolism): FPN1 export of Fe2+ at top left, TfR1 and transferrin-bound Fe3+ at top, endosome with STEAP3 and DMT1, labile iron pool box, ferritin storage and ferritinophagy at left, heme from a mitochondrion at right, and at the bottom the line Fe2+ + H2O2 to Fe3+ + OH- + OH-.

entries.proposition: Figure 4 is a conceptual two-loop schematic (seizure to glutamate to System Xc- to GSH to GPX4 to lipid peroxidation to cell death; iron overload to Fenton to ROS to network excitability) with yellow stars at intervention points and no data, axes or citations inside the panel.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation - pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 4: red-arrow loop from epileptic seizure through glutamate release, System Xc- inhibition, depletion of GSH, inactivation of GPX4, lipid peroxidation and neuronal cell death back to seizure; blue-arrow loop from iron overload through a Fenton reaction labelled 'Fe+ - Fention reaction' to ROS, neuronal overexcitation and synaptic disorders to the epilepsy network; stars on iron overload, GPX4 and ROS; no numeric data.
